chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him: A mukatab (a slave who has contracted for his manumission) bought his own freedom and left behind property worth one hundred thousand dirhams, and he had no heir. He said: 'The one who assumes his blood-money liability inherits him.' I said: 'Who is the one who assumes liability for his blood-money?' He said: 'The one who assumes liability for the blood-guilt of the Muslims.'

key_terms.اَلضَّامِنُ: The guarantor or one who assumes liability.
key_terms.جَرَائِرِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ: The blood-guilt/liabilities of the Muslims (referring to the collective responsibility).
key_terms.جَرِيرَتُهُ: His blood-money liability or debt of blood-guilt.
key_terms.مُكَاتَبٌ: A slave who has entered into a contract to buy his freedom by paying a specified sum to his master.

ai.seo_question: Who inherits a mukatab who dies without heirs?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that the heir of a *mukatab* (slave who has contracted for freedom) without direct descendants is the guarantor of his *diyah* (blood-money), a role traditionally held by the Muslim community or the Imam. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that financial liability for a person's life entitles the payer to their estate, effectively treating the community as a legal heir in the absence of kin. It highlights the interconnectedness of *diyah* and inheritance law in classical Shia fiqh.
